claims.claim: Interactions among the VCSC glia, basement membrane and epidermal cells reflect the genetic relationships uncovered in the forward genetic screens.
claims.source: Interactions among the VCSC glia, basement membrane and epidermal cells reflect the genetic relationships we uncovered in our forward genetic screens, as epidermal CIMA-1 and EGL-15/FGFR modulate glia morphology through epidermal-glial adhesion, and secreted MIG-17 modulate glia morphology through the muscle-derived extracellular matrix.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the anatomical observations with the genetic findings.

claims.claim: The muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis described here is reminiscent of the neurovascular unit of the blood-brain barrier in Drosophila and vertebrates.
claims.source: The muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis described here is reminiscent of the neurovascular unit of the blood-brain barrier in Drosophila and vertebrates.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison drawn by the authors.

claims.claim: In the vertebrate neurovascular unit, muscle-related pericyte cells interact with vascular endothelial cells and astrocytes through the basement membrane.
claims.source: In the vertebrate neurovascular unit, muscle-related pericyte cells interact with vascular endothelial cells and astrocytes through the basement membrane (Xu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Pericytes, endothelial cells and the basement membrane are not in direct contact with neurons.
claims.source: Pericytes, endothelial cells and the basement membrane are not in direct contact with neurons.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the neurovascular unit.

claims.claim: Astrocytes mediate signaling between pericytes, endothelial cells, basement membrane and neurons.
claims.source: Instead, astrocytes mediate signaling between these non-neuronal cells and neurons, including coupling the developmental programs that coordinate vasculature development and neurodevelopment (Tam and Watts, 2010), and the functional programs that coordinate neuronal activity with blood flow (Allan, 2006; Koehler et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The extracellular matrix of the blood-brain barrier is molecularly similar to the basement membrane of C. elegans, and includes molecules such as laminin, collagen IV and fibulin.
claims.source: We note that the extracellular matrix of the blood-brain barrier is molecularly similar to the basement membrane of C. elegans, and includes molecules we tested here, such as laminin, collagen IV and fibulin (Thomsen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The functional neurovascular unit may transduce information from the vasculature to sustain synaptic positions during allometric growth.
claims.source: While the role of these components in vertebrate synaptic allometry has not been examined, we speculate that the functional neurovascular unit may transduce information from the vasculature to sustain synaptic positions during allometric growth.
claims.evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on the parallels they draw.

claims.claim: Analogous structures in other organisms may represent conserved signaling axis that couple glia-mediated communication among non-neuronal cells and neurons to position synapses.
claims.source: Our findings therefore uncover a novel muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis, which communicates in part through the remodeling of the basement membrane to sustains synaptic specificity during the organism's allometric growth. We hypothesize that analogous structures in other organisms may represent conserved signaling axis that couple glia-mediated communication among non-neuronal cells and neurons to position synapses.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

results.result: Forward genetic screens identified mig-17, encoding a conserved ADAMTS metalloprotease, as a suppressor of cima-1(wy84) synaptic allometry defects. Multiple loss-of-function alleles (ola226, k113, k174) suppress ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1 mutants, and wild-type mig-17 rescues the suppression phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C44, C57, C93-C101 provide converging genetic evidence that mig-17 is the gene responsible for suppression. The identification through forward genetics (C4, C57), molecular characterization (C93-C95), phenotypic analysis of multiple alleles (C96-C98), and rescue experiments (C99-C100) collectively support this result with appropriate statistical significance (p<0.0001).

results.result: The ola226 allele suppresses synaptic allometry defects in cima-1(wy84) mutants by restoring glia position and morphology. In double mutants, ectopic presynaptic sites are reduced from 93.9% to 54.6% (p<0.0001), glia anterior process length is reduced from 127.53 μm to 120.68 μm (p<0.0001), and abnormal AIY-glia contact is reduced from 88.70% to 33.67% (p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C82 provide quantitative evidence with appropriate statistical tests showing that ola226 suppresses both synaptic and glia morphology phenotypes in cima-1 mutants. The measurements are internally consistent and supported by microscopy images (C76, C79, C81). Sample sizes appear adequate (N>40 for most measurements).

results.result: In cima-1(wy84) mutants, VCSC glia are posteriorly displaced with longer anterior processes (127.53 μm vs 113.35 μm in wild type, p<0.0001) and extended endfeet (51.47 μm vs 45.52 μm, p<0.0001), resulting in ectopic presynaptic sites. Glia ablation suppresses the ectopic presynaptic phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 provide quantitative morphological measurements with appropriate statistics and are supported by microscopy data (C69, C71). The ablation experiment (C74) provides functional evidence linking glia position to the synaptic phenotype, though this relies on a citation to previous work.

results.result: ola226 mutants show anterior displacement of both VCSC glia and AIY neurons (opposite to cima-1 phenotype), but maintain normal overlap between glia and AIY, resulting in wild-type synaptic patterns. This demonstrates that relative position between glia and AIY, rather than absolute position, drives presynaptic positioning during growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C92 provide a critical insight supported by quantitative measurements showing that ola226 mutants have altered absolute positions but normal relative positions and synaptic patterns. The inference about relative positioning (C91) is well-supported by the data showing that both cells move together while maintaining proper synaptic patterns (C89-C90).

results.result: MIG-17 is expressed in body wall muscles and neurons but not in glia or epidermal cells. Expression from either muscle or neuronal promoters rescues the cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) phenotype, consistent with MIG-17 being a secreted ADAMTS protease.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 are supported by reporter expression data (C107-C109) and rescue experiments (C110, C112). The conclusion that MIG-17 is secreted (C111, C113) is well-supported by the ability of expression from multiple cell types to rescue the phenotype, consistent with known properties of ADAMTS proteases.

results.result: MIG-17 metalloprotease enzymatic activity is required for promoting ectopic synapse formation in cima-1(wy84) mutants. The engineered catalytic mutant mig-17(shc8[E303A]) suppresses ectopic synapses (91.91% to 57.49%, p<0.0001), and a transgene with the E303A mutation cannot rescue the suppression phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 provide strong evidence for the requirement of enzymatic activity through both loss-of-function (C114-C115) and rescue failure (C116) experiments. The use of a catalytic site mutant is appropriate for testing enzymatic function. The inference that MIG-17 remodels basement membrane (C118) is reasonable given the enzymatic requirement and known ADAMTS functions.

results.result: MIG-17 regulates basement membrane protein levels, with multiple components upregulated in mig-17(ola226) mutants including EMB-9/Collagen IV, UNC-52/Perlecan, and laminins. Neomorphic/hypomorphic emb-9 alleles, loss-of-function unc-52 alleles, and gain-of-function fbl-1 alleles all suppress cima-1(wy84) ectopic synapses, suggesting altered basement membrane properties prevent glia repositioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C136 are supported by proteomic mass spectrometry data (C119-C120) and genetic epistasis experiments (C126, C130, C132, C134). The genetic interactions are internally consistent and support the model that basement membrane alterations suppress glia movement. However, the proteomic data would benefit from more detailed statistical analysis and validation of specific proteins.

results.result: MIG-17 and EMB-9 protein levels are inversely regulated during post-embryonic growth. MIG-17 is detectable in larval stages but undetectable in adults, while EMB-9 increases through larval stages to maximal expression in adults. EMB-9::mCherry levels are upregulated in mig-17(ola226) mutants, indicating MIG-17 regulates EMB-9 and basement membrane properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C146 are supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements at different developmental stages (C139-C140) and in different genetic backgrounds (C143-C144). The temporal expression patterns (C141) and genetic regulation (C143) support the inference that MIG-17 regulates EMB-9 (C142, C146). The observation that cima-1 also affects EMB-9 levels (C144-C145) suggests additional complexity.

results.result: MIG-17 and EGL-15/FGFR genetically interact in the same pathway to regulate synaptic allometry. mig-17 and egl-15 loss-of-function alleles similarly suppress cima-1 without enhancing each other, and mig-17(ola226) suppresses the effects of EGL-15(5A)/FGFR overexpression, indicating mig-17 is epistatic to egl-15.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C163 provide genetic epistasis data showing that mig-17 and egl-15 act in related pathways (C152-C154) and that mig-17 is epistatic to egl-15 (C158-C162). The data support the model that MIG-17 modifies basement membrane to modulate CIMA-1/EGL-15 regulated epidermal-glial crosstalk (C163). The epistasis analysis is appropriate and well-supported.

results.result: Electron microscopy reveals that VCSC glia have three distinct surface regions: direct contact with neurons on the nerve ring-facing side, direct contact with epidermal cells on the pseudocoelom-facing side, and contact with muscle-derived basement membrane also on the pseudocoelom-facing side. This anatomical arrangement supports a muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis that sustains synaptic allometry during growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C179 are supported by electron microscopy images showing the anatomical relationships between glia, neurons, epidermis, and basement membrane (C165-C170). The inference that this anatomy supports a multi-tissue signaling axis (C171-C174, C179) is well-supported by the combination of anatomical and functional genetic data. The model integrates multiple lines of evidence coherently.

results.result: A muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis, modulated by MIG-17 and the basement membrane, sustains synaptic specificity during allometric growth. Secreted MIG-17 dynamically regulates muscle-derived basement membrane, which modulates CIMA-1-dependent epidermal-glial crosstalk to regulate glia position and morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C147-C148, C163, C174-C175, C206 represent the main conclusion synthesized from multiple lines of evidence including genetics, proteomics, cell biology, and anatomy. The model is well-supported by the collective findings, though it represents an inference integrating multiple observations rather than a single direct measurement. The conclusion appropriately synthesizes the major findings.

results.result: In wild-type animals, the AIY synaptic pattern is sustained from L1 to adults despite order-of-magnitude growth. In cima-1(wy84) mutants, the embryonic pattern develops correctly but ectopic presynaptic sites emerge during growth. The ola226 allele does not affect synaptogenesis in young animals but suppresses post-embryonic synaptic allometry defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C49, C51-C52, C58-C59 establish the basic phenotypes and are supported by microscopy images at different developmental stages. The distinction between developmental and growth-related defects is important for the study's conclusions and is well-documented. These observations provide the foundation for the genetic screens.

results.result: The suppression of cima-1(wy84) by ola226 is not due to changes in body size, as ola226 and cima-1(wy84);ola226 animals are indistinguishable from wild-type in length. However, body size affects the expressivity of cima-1(wy84) phenotypes, with shorter dpy mutants suppressing and longer lon mutants enhancing the defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68, C64-C66 provide important controls showing that ola226's effects are not simply due to altered body size (C67-C68), while demonstrating that growth does affect phenotype expressivity (C64-C66). The measurements are quantitative with appropriate statistics. This distinguishes the specific mechanism of ola226 from general growth effects.

results.result: Sustaining synaptic allometry depends on the relative position between glia and AIY neurons rather than their absolute positions. When both cells are mispositioned but maintain their contact relationship, correct synaptic allometry is sustained, demonstrating glia act as guideposts during growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C185, C91-C92 represent a key conceptual insight supported by the ola226 phenotype data. The inference is well-supported by observations that absolute positions can change while relative positions and synaptic patterns remain normal (C185). This is an important mechanistic insight about how synaptic positions are maintained during growth.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that altered basement membrane properties in mig-17 and emb-9 mutants prevent glia movement during growth, suppressing ectopic contacts between glia and AIY in cima-1 mutants. This inability to reposition does not disrupt synaptic allometry when the glia-AIY relationship is preserved, but defects occur when this relationship is altered.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129, C136, C202-C205 represent a mechanistic hypothesis supported by the genetic data showing that multiple basement membrane perturbations suppress cima-1. The model is reasonable and consistent with the data, though it represents an inference about mechanism rather than direct demonstration. The hypothesis could be strengthened with direct measurements of basement membrane material properties or glia mobility.

results.result: The mechanisms that sustain synaptic specificity during allometric growth, particularly how the basement membrane sustains CNS neuron-neuron synapses during brain allometric growth, are largely unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C19, C23 establish the knowledge gap that motivates the study. These are reasonable assessments of the field based on the limited prior work on synaptic maintenance during growth versus development. This provides appropriate context for the study's significance.

results.result: The authors draw parallels between the muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis in C. elegans and the neurovascular unit of the blood-brain barrier in vertebrates, speculating that analogous structures may represent conserved signaling axes coupling glia-mediated communication among non-neuronal cells and neurons to position synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C213-C219 represent comparative speculation about conservation across species. While the molecular similarities are noted (C217), the functional parallels are speculative (C218-C219). The comparison is reasonable and potentially insightful, but lacks direct experimental support. This represents a hypothesis for future work rather than a supported conclusion from the current study.

results.result: Background claims establishing that synaptic positions underlie circuit connectivity, can be established during embryogenesis and sustained during growth, and that non-neuronal cells and ECM are important for synaptic specificity. C. elegans provides a tractable model for studying these processes during allometric growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C13-C18, C20-C22, C24-C29 represent established knowledge from the field supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary background and context for the study. The claims about C. elegans as a model system (C27-C29) are well-established and appropriate.

results.result: Previous work identified cima-1 as required for sustaining synaptic patterns during growth. CIMA-1 functions in epidermal cells to antagonize EGL-15/FGFR, which acts as an extracellular adhesion factor to modulate epidermal-glial adhesion and glia morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36, C38-C41, C149-C151, C157 summarize previous work from the authors and others, supported by appropriate citations. These establish the foundation for the current study and are necessary context. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: MIG-17 is an ADAMTS metalloprotease known for roles in gonad development and pharyngeal growth. Unlike NMJs where basement membrane directly contacts synapses, the basement membrane in the nerve ring does not directly contact AIY synapses, suggesting MIG-17 modulates synaptic allometry through effects on glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 combine established knowledge about MIG-17 (C102-C103) with anatomical observations (C104) to make an inference about mechanism (C105-C106). The inference is reasonable given the anatomical constraints and is supported by the subsequent functional data. This sets up the key mechanistic question addressed by the study.

results.result: Previous work demonstrated that VCSC glia play critical roles in both embryonic development (through Netrin secretion) and post-embryonic growth (through Netrin-independent pathways) to sustain presynaptic positions. The current study extends these findings to highlight glia's role in sustaining synaptic patterns during allometric growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C183, C186-C187 summarize previous work on glia function and place the current study in context. The claims are supported by appropriate citations and the extension to allometric growth (C187) is a reasonable characterization of the current study's contribution.

results.result: Growth in C. elegans relies on coordinated signals from epidermal cells and body wall muscles. The study uncovers a cooperative signaling pathway from these growth-regulating cell types that positions glia to drive synaptic positioning during allometry, with secreted MIG-17 epistatic to epidermally derived CIMA-1 and EGL-15/FGFR.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C192, C194 integrate established knowledge about C. elegans growth (C188-C190) with the study's findings about the signaling pathway (C191-C192, C194). The inference about a cooperative pathway is well-supported by the genetic epistasis data. This represents an important conceptual advance in understanding how growth information is transduced to the nervous system.

results.result: ADAMTS metalloproteases function to degrade and remodel the extracellular matrix and are important for nervous system development and maintenance across species. The proteomic, genetic, and cell biological findings suggest the basement membrane is a dynamic structure that remodels, with MIG-17 regulating synaptic allometry by modulating the basement membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C195-C201 combine established knowledge about ADAMTS function (C195-C198) with the study's findings (C199-C201). The inference that the basement membrane is dynamic and remodels (C199) is well-supported by the proteomic data showing changes in basement membrane protein levels and the genetic data showing effects of basement membrane perturbations.

results.result: Unlike NMJs which directly contact basement membrane, neurons in the nerve ring are not in direct contact with basement membrane. Instead, VCSC glia ensheath the nerve ring, contacting neurons on one side and either basement membrane or epidermal cells on the other, reflecting the genetic relationships uncovered in the screens.
results.evaluation: Claims C207-C212 establish important anatomical distinctions between NMJs and nerve ring synapses (C207-C209) and describe the glia's position (C210-C211). The connection between anatomy and genetics (C212) is a reasonable inference supported by the data. This anatomical context is crucial for understanding how basement membrane affects synapses indirectly through glia.
